keyScripture.why: I was a stranger and you welcomed me, placing the welcome of the outsider at the center of the last judgment and identifying Christ himself with the stranger at the door, so that the cost of the open door is paid, unaware, to him.

discussion.q: Bell says it is one thing to admire Abraham and another to answer the door, and the stranger now is the lonely widow, the immigrant, the coworker no one sits with. Who is the actual stranger in your actual life that this session is asking about?
discussion.behind: Open by making it concrete and unavoidable. The whole study can stay safely biblical until this moment, when it lands on a real person the reader already knows and avoids. Push past the abstract stranger to the named one, the specific lonely or foreign or inconvenient person already in their orbit. That person is the session.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case for boundaries, that no one can meet every need and limitless compassion collapses the giver. What is true in that, and where has the language of boundaries become your permanent excuse?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves with real honesty. Limits are wise and burnout helps no one, and the study honors the boundary. But boundaries is also the most fluent modern excuse, the therapeutic-sounding reason the door happens to stay shut against everyone. Help the room tell the difference between a real limit and a fear that has learned to speak the language of self-care.

discussion.q: Scripture says love the sojourner, for you were sojourners, naming the immigrant as an object of God's particular care. Why do you think this specific command is one the church most easily explains away?
discussion.behind: Press gently but do not flinch, and keep it pastoral rather than partisan. The command about the sojourner is unusually explicit and unusually ignored, and the reasons are often political rather than biblical. The point is not to score a side but to notice how readily we let the culture's fears overwrite a clear and repeated command. Diagnose the evasion in ourselves first, not in the other tribe.

discussion.q: Bell says every real welcome costs the host something, and a welcome that costs nothing was never what Scripture meant. What has hospitality actually cost you, and what cost have you been unwilling to pay?
discussion.behind: Move toward the center, the cost. The cheap welcome that risks and spends nothing is the counterfeit, and the room should feel that the real thing has a price, time, comfort, safety, the tidy life. Let people name both what they have paid and what they have refused to, and keep the leader inside the question, naming their own unpaid cost first.

discussion.q: Bell says we were welcomed at infinite cost, by a host who set the table with his own body. How does the cost of your welcome look different held against the cost of the welcome you received?
discussion.behind: Close on the gospel and let the weight stand unresolved. Every cost we count in welcoming the stranger is small against the cost God paid to welcome us. The point is not to shame the room into more effort but to reframe the cost as an echo of grace. End in weight, not in a plan, and let the threshold and the decision be the last thing in the room.

objections.objection: You have to have boundaries. No one can help everyone, and people who try to meet every need burn out, neglect their own families, and end up useless to anybody. Endless open-door hospitality is a recipe for exhaustion and resentment.
objections.response: Grant it, because it is true and the study means the grant. Limits are real and wise, no one can meet every need, the person who tries to save everyone saves no one and often wrecks their own household in the attempt, and Peter's without grumbling already warns against the welcome that curdles into resentment. Hold the boundary honestly. Where the objection needs pressing is the ease with which boundaries becomes a word that blesses a door that was already shut, the language of self-care laid over a self-protection that was never going to open anyway. A real limit says I can welcome this one and not that one this month. A false one says I have boundaries and welcomes no one, ever, and calls the coldness wisdom. The test is simple and uncomfortable. If your boundaries have never once been crossed by an actual costly welcome, they are not boundaries protecting a generous life, they are walls protecting a closed one.

objections.objection: Immigration is a complicated political and legal issue, and you cannot just quote love the sojourner as though it settles questions of borders and law and national policy. Using Scripture that way is naive and ignores real concerns about security and fairness.
objections.response: Concede the real complexity first, because it is genuine and the study is not pretending otherwise. Questions of law, of borders, of national policy are legitimately hard, they involve competing goods and real concerns about security and fairness, and Scripture does not hand anyone a finished immigration policy, and this is not legal or political advice. Grant all of that plainly. But notice the move the objection is tempted to make, from the policy is complicated, which is true, to the command does not apply to me, which does not follow. Whatever a nation's laws should be, the individual believer still meets an actual sojourner, a real family, a real neighbor, a real stranger, and to that person Scripture is not vague at all. Love the sojourner, for you were sojourners. The complexity of the policy question is real, and it is also, very often, the respectable fog we hide in to avoid the simple and personal command that was never about policy in the first place, only about the stranger in front of you.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Name the stranger you have decided not to welcome, and name honestly the cost you were unwilling to pay, and ask whether the reason is a real limit or a locked door wearing the language of wisdom.
sessions.practice: This week, take the one named stranger this session brought to mind, the lonely, the immigrant, the outsider you already know, and pay one real cost to welcome them, an afternoon, a meal, a lasting inconvenience, something that actually costs you. Do not solve their whole life. Cross one threshold. And name to God the cost you have been refusing, and ask whether it is a boundary or a wall. Write down who it was, what it cost, and what you found on the other side of the open door.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you were the stranger, and you told us that when we welcomed the least of these we welcomed you, and that when we shut the door we shut it on you. We have admired Abraham and locked our own doors. We have used the language of boundaries to bless a coldness we were never going to warm, and the language of complexity to excuse ourselves from a command that was always simple and personal. Forgive us the strangers we have decided not to see, the lonely, the foreigner, the outsider you named and we ignored. You welcomed us at infinite cost, setting the table with your own body while we were still far off. Give us the courage of an open door and the willingness to pay what welcome costs, because grace was never cheap and neither is the love that echoes it. Amen.
reflection: Who is the specific stranger, the lonely or foreign or inconvenient person, that I already know and have quietly decided not to welcome?
Where has the language of boundaries become a wall, a self-protection that was never going to open no matter what?
What has my welcome actually cost me, and what cost am I refusing, and how does it look against the cost God paid to welcome me?
sessions.teaching: It is one thing to admire Abraham running in the heat, and quite another to answer your own door. So the last session takes hospitality down out of the pages of Scripture, out of the tents and the upper rooms, and sets it on the street where the reader actually lives, because that is where the whole thing was always heading and where it is easiest to avoid. The stranger, in your life, is not a picturesque traveler with a robe and a staff. The stranger is the widow across the hall who has not had a visitor in weeks and whose television you can hear through the wall. The stranger is the immigrant family down the block that the neighborhood has quietly decided not to see, whose English is halting and whose need is real. The stranger is the coworker no one eats lunch with, the new family at church nobody invited home, the person whose presence is inconvenient and whose loneliness is a fact. And once the stranger has a face, the question changes. It is no longer what hospitality means, a question we can discuss all day without moving. It is what hospitality costs, because Scripture never once pretends the open door is free. Take the strong case for boundaries first, because it is wise and the study will not caricature it into selfishness. No one can meet every need. The person who tries to save everyone ends by saving no one, neglecting their own family, running themselves into the ground until they have nothing left to give anyone. Compassion without limits does not scale into sainthood, it collapses into breakdown, and there is real foolishness in the guilt-driven welcome that ignores every cost until it destroys the one giving it. Peter himself guarded against the welcome that turns to resentment. Grant all of that. Limits are not the enemy of love, they are sometimes its discipline. But now watch how fast the wise thing becomes the excuse, because it does, and I know the trick from the inside. Boundaries is the most fluent word in the modern vocabulary, and it will bless almost anything. It can name a real limit that protects a genuinely generous life, and it can, just as easily, lay a coat of therapeutic language over a door that was already shut and was never going to open, and the two sound exactly alike from the outside. The test is uncomfortable and it is simple. If your boundaries have never once been crossed by an actual costly welcome, if they have only ever kept people out and never been spent on anyone, then they are not boundaries protecting a generous life. They are walls protecting a closed one, and calling themselves wisdom. Then the study has to name the strangers our own moment most wants to turn away, and it will not be vague, because Scripture is not. Over and over, with a frequency that should embarrass us, the law and the prophets return to the sojourner, the foreigner, the immigrant, the one who is not from here. You shall love the sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. You shall not wrong a stranger or oppress him. When a stranger sojourns with you, you shall treat him as the native among you, and love him as yourself. This is not a modern political question that Scripture happens to be silent on. It is a named and repeated object of God's particular care, and the church that turns its face from the outsider has turned its face from a command it cannot honestly pretend it did not read. Yes, the policy questions are genuinely hard, the law and the border and the national interest are real and complicated, and none of this is a tidy answer to any of that, nor legal advice, nor a party's talking point. But notice the move we are all tempted to make, the slide from the policy is complicated, which is true, straight to the command does not touch me, which does not follow at all. Whatever the law should be, you still meet an actual sojourner, a real family, a real face, and to that person Scripture could not be less vague. And here is where I stand inside it, because I have used every one of these excuses. I have hidden in the complexity of the issue to avoid the simplicity of the person. I have called my locked door a boundary. I have admired the biblical strangers and declined the ones on my own street. So the reversal that ends the whole study is not a technique and not a program, and I will not tie it off with a clean application, because the subject will not allow it. Every real welcome costs the host something. It costs time you wanted for yourself, comfort you would rather keep, safety you cannot fully guarantee, the tidy and defended life you have built. A welcome that costs the host nothing was never the thing Scripture meant by the word. And the reason we know that, the thing that takes the whole matter out of the realm of nice gestures and lays it on us with full weight, is that we were welcomed at infinite cost. God did not open his door cheaply. He set the table with his own body, welcomed us while we were still strangers and enemies and far off, and paid for the seat we could never afford with the life of his Son. I was a stranger, Christ says, standing at the last judgment, and you welcomed me, or you did not. The open door is expensive because grace was expensive. And so the study ends, not with a plan for you to execute, but with a threshold in front of you and a stranger on the other side of it, and a decision that no one, in the end, can make for you.

scriptureStudy.note: I was a stranger and you welcomed me, as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me. Christ identifies himself with the stranger so fully that the welcome of the outsider is the welcome of God, and its refusal is the refusal of God.

He loves the sojourner, giving him food and clothing. Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners. God's own care for the foreigner is made the ground and the pattern of Israel's, and the memory of being strangers is the engine of the command.

When a stranger sojourns with you, you shall not do him wrong, you shall love him as yourself. The command to love your neighbor as yourself is here extended explicitly to the foreigner, closing the loophole that would keep love inside the tribe.

The sojourner has not lodged in the street, I have opened my doors to the traveler. Job offers his open door as evidence of a righteous life, treating hospitality to the stranger not as an extra but as a basic mark of integrity before God.

Is not this the fast that I choose, to bring the homeless poor into your house. God rejects a piety that will not open its home, naming the welcome of the destitute as the worship he actually wants and the empty religion he refuses.

A Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and he had compassion, and took care of him. The despised outsider becomes the model of costly welcome, paying real money and real time for a stranger, while the respectable pass by on the other side.

Welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God. Paul grounds every human welcome in the divine one, making our open door an echo of Christ's, measured not by what it costs us but by the infinite cost of the welcome we received.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the two hard edges this session lives on, the cost of welcome and the particular stranger of the immigrant, because both are places the church's practice most often fails and most often rationalizes. On cost, take up Christine Pohl's argument in Making Room that genuine hospitality has always been costly and even risky, that the historic Christian practice welcomed the stranger without a guarantee of safety or reward, and that our modern insistence on a fully controlled and risk-free welcome may be precisely what has hollowed the practice out. A group can weigh, carefully and without recklessness, the difference between prudence and the total risk-aversion that has made real hospitality nearly impossible, and ask what it would mean to accept some genuine cost and uncertainty as intrinsic to the thing rather than a failure of planning. On the sojourner, take up the sheer weight of the biblical material, the more than thirty explicit commands concerning the ger, the resident foreigner, and set it against the church's frequent silence or hostility, asking honestly whether our politics has overwritten our exegesis. This must be handled the way the platform handles every contested question, refusing to baptize a party and refusing to flee the text, granting that policy is genuinely hard and second-order while insisting that the personal command to love the actual sojourner is neither. Then take the final turn, the one Nouwen and Pohl both press toward, that hospitality is ultimately eschatological, a foretaste of the great feast where people come from east and west and north and south to sit at one table, so that every open door now is a small rehearsal of the kingdom then, and every closed one a quiet denial of it. The aim is to send the reader out not with a technique but with a changed sight, able to see in the stranger at the door the Christ who was himself a stranger, and to count the cost of welcome against the cost of the welcome that saved them.
sessions.caseStudy: A couple in your group has genuinely welcomed people over the years, and they are tired, and they say, with real weariness rather than excuse-making, that they have given and given and been taken advantage of, and that they have learned they need boundaries now. They are not cold, they have scars from actually opening the door. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor the scars before it presses anything. They are not the closed-door people the session warns about, they have paid real costs, and their weariness is earned and their need for limits is legitimate, and you must say so plainly and mean it, because to lecture the genuinely spent about generosity is its own cruelty. But notice, gently, the difference between the boundaries of a generous life that needs to recover and the boundaries that quietly close the door for good, and help them tell which they are near. The wise limit says not now, or not this one, or not alone. The wall says never again, and dresses the wound as a policy. Honor their exhaustion fully, protect their need for rest, and still ask them, when they are ready, whether the door is closing to heal or closing to stay closed, because a hospitality that has cost them this much is worth grieving over and worth, in time and with wisdom, opening again.

memoryVerse.text: As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.

leaderPrimer: The particular danger of a hospitality study is that it is the easiest study in the world to enjoy and never obey. It is warm, it is winsome, it flatters us with images of open tables and welcomed strangers, and a room can spend five weeks admiring Abraham and the early church and Jesus among the sinners and go home having opened not a single door. Admiration is the counterfeit of obedience, and it is especially seductive here, because the subject is so pleasant to discuss. So set the rule the first night and hold it. This study is not finished when we understand hospitality. It is finished when someone in this room has actually welcomed a stranger, and every session drives toward a threshold in the real life of a real person, not toward a nice idea about welcome in general. Keep pulling the discussion off the abstract stranger and onto the named one, the actual lonely or foreign or inconvenient person each member already knows and already avoids. That person is the point of the whole thing. Watch for two failure modes. The first is the showroom instinct, the members who cannot imagine welcoming anyone because their home is not nice enough or their life not tidy enough, and who need to hear, again and again, that hospitality is not entertaining, that a plain table in a plain room is exactly the thing, that the introvert and the poor and the overwhelmed are commanded and equipped for this as much as anyone. The second is the fortress instinct, the members who have quietly decided their home is a private sanctuary the world does not enter, and who will need the gentle, persistent pressure of the actual biblical commands. Handle the fifth session with particular care, because it names the immigrant and the outsider plainly and some of that will run into people's politics. Keep it pastoral and personal rather than partisan, diagnose the evasion in the room and in yourself before anyone else, grant that policy is genuinely hard, and refuse to let the complexity of the policy become the fog that hides the simplicity of the person. Bell leads this from inside it. He came to faith from atheism and was welcomed to a table before he believed, and he knows the fortress reflex because it is his own. If you present yourself as the hospitable expert, the room will admire you and change nothing. Go in as someone still learning to open a door that keeps wanting to stay shut. Five weeks will not turn a group into the early church. It can turn admiration into a first open door, and send a few people home to set one more place at the table for someone who cannot pay them back.

faq.q: Is this study going to make people feel guilty for not having a nice enough home to host?
faq.a: The opposite is the whole aim of the first session. The study attacks head-on the great modern substitution that turned hospitality into entertaining, a performance staged in a presentable home for guests who are expected to stage one back. Scripture does not use a word for the dinner party, it uses philoxenia, love of the stranger, and it assumes a plain table in a plain room. The showroom standard has crushed more welcome than selfishness ever has, because people who cannot host beautifully often decide not to host at all, letting a good thing, the lovely gathering, become the enemy of the commanded thing, the open door. The study insists that the introvert, the poor, and the overwhelmed are commanded and equipped for hospitality as much as anyone, and that the stranger needs a chair, not a showroom. No one should finish this study feeling their home is not good enough. They should finish freed from the standard that told them so.

faq.q: What is the difference between hospitality and entertaining, and why does the study make so much of it?
faq.a: Entertaining is a performance staged for people who can return the favor, a gathering of friends in a presentable home, and it runs, quietly, on reciprocity, the ledger of invitations given and expected back. Hospitality, the word Scripture actually uses, is philoxenia, love of the stranger, the xenos, the one who cannot repay you. Jesus drew the line himself, telling a host not to invite the friends and rich neighbors who will invite him back, but the poor who cannot. The study makes much of it because the substitution is nearly invisible and it changes what we think God is asking. Entertaining is a good thing, the feast of friends is a real gift, and the study does not despise it. But it is not the same as the command, and when the circle only ever seats the people who can seat us back, we have kept something smaller and more comfortable than what Scripture meant, and called it hospitality.

faq.q: Does the study say it is wrong to have friends over for dinner?
faq.a: No, and it says so plainly. Gathering friends around a table is one of the good gifts of this life, a foretaste of the wedding feast, and there is nothing false or second-rate about the joy of it. The study is not asking anyone to stop enjoying their friends or to turn every meal into a mission with an agenda. What it presses on is not the meal with friends but the meal that is only ever with friends, the circle that never once opens to the stranger who cannot repay. Keep the feast of friends, the study says, and add the empty chair for the one who cannot give anything back, and you have both the joy of friendship and the shape of the gospel at the same table. The problem is never the friends. It is the closed circle that never becomes anything more.

faq.q: Is it not naive and even dangerous to tell people to welcome strangers into their homes?
faq.a: The study takes the danger seriously and does not counsel recklessness. Wisdom is a virtue, not a failure of love, and no one should hear this as a demand to put children or the vulnerable in harm's way, and discernment about a specific person in a specific situation is not the same as a closed heart. Abraham welcomed eagerly, not carelessly, and the two are not the same. What the study presses on is the slide from a real and specific caution into a general and permanent one, where the rare danger of the predator becomes the settled excuse that keeps the door shut against every ordinary stranger who was never a threat at all. The task is not to abandon wisdom but to refuse to let a rare danger justify a permanent coldness, to keep the door that discernment opens rather than the one fear locks. Prudence is real. It is also the most respectable cover a closed heart ever wears, and the study asks the reader to tell the two apart honestly.

faq.q: Why does the study spend a whole session on who Jesus ate with?
faq.a: Because the table Jesus kept was the single most repeated complaint against him, and it turns out to be the center of the gospel, not a charming detail. This man receives sinners and eats with them was an accusation, and it is accidentally the best summary of Christianity in the Bible. In that world a shared meal declared acceptance, so when Jesus ate with tax collectors and the unclean he was saying, with his body, that the kingdom comes to people before they clean themselves up, not after. He did not lower the standard, he relocated the healing, insisting the table is where the sick get well and a physician goes to the sick, not the healthy. The session presses the reader to see that their own table, sorted quietly by who deserves a chair, is more like the critics than like Christ, and that we were all seated by a host who ate with us while we were still his enemies.

faq.q: Does welcoming everyone mean the church has no standards and approves of everything?
faq.a: No, and the study guards against exactly that distortion. Jesus did not treat sin as nothing, he called people to repentance and told the woman to go and sin no more, and a welcome that quietly approves of everything has stopped being love and become mere permissiveness. The friend of sinners line has indeed been abused as cover by churches that simply lacked the nerve to say anything hard, and that is a betrayal of the very Jesus they invoke. But the cure for a limp welcome is not a closed one. Jesus held both at once, the open table and the hard word, and told the truth from inside the welcome, never from across the room. The order matters. Respectability says clean up and then come to the table. Jesus says come to the table, and here is where you get clean. The go and sin no more comes after the welcome, never as its price of entry.

faq.q: What does the study mean by calling the church a household?
faq.a: It means that for the first three hundred years the church had no buildings at all. It met in homes, ate in homes, welcomed the stranger and the traveler into homes, and the open door was not a program the church ran but the shape of what the church was. Paul lists hospitality in Romans 12 alongside genuine love and blessing your enemies, using a word that means to pursue it, to hunt for someone to welcome. Acts describes Christians breaking bread in their homes day by day with glad and generous hearts. The study honors what the modern church gained in buildings and programs and organized care at scale, which reach further than any single table. But it names what was lost when welcome moved entirely from the home to the agency, the stranger becoming a client, the welcome becoming a transaction, no actual threshold ever crossed. The household of God was a household, and the door was the point.

faq.q: I am exhausted and introverted. Is this just going to guilt me into burning out?
faq.a: No, and the study works hard against that reading. Rest is a genuine good, God himself rested, the tired and the introverted are not disqualified from the kingdom, and a hospitality that produces burnout and resentment has already failed the without grumbling that Peter attached to it. The study clears away the false version first, the pressure to run a constant open house that no one could sustain. The early church's homes were ordinary and tired and full of children too, and the open door never meant the door never closed, only that it was not permanently locked against the stranger. One guest is not a program. Once a month is not burnout. The introvert can welcome one person deeply, which is often truer hospitality than a crowded room. The command is not to exhaust yourself but to refuse the fortress, to let your ordinary home, rest and all, have a door that sometimes opens, which is a rhythm a tired person can actually keep.

faq.q: How does the study handle immigration without becoming political?
faq.a: Carefully, and by drawing a clear line between two questions the culture keeps blurring. The study concedes plainly that immigration policy is genuinely hard, that questions of law and borders and national interest involve competing goods and real concerns, that Scripture does not hand anyone a finished policy, and that none of this is legal or political advice. It refuses to baptize a party. But it also refuses to let the complexity of the policy question become the fog that hides a command that was never about policy. Whatever a nation's laws should be, the individual believer still meets an actual sojourner, a real family, a real neighbor, and to that person Scripture could not be less vague, love the sojourner, for you were sojourners. The study diagnoses the evasion in the church and in the writer first, not in the other tribe, and keeps the fifth session pastoral and personal rather than partisan, pressing the simple and personal command rather than the contested and political one.

faq.q: Is hospitality really a command, or just a nice thing for people who enjoy it?
faq.a: It is a command, laid on the whole church and not on a gifted subset. Romans commands it, Hebrews commands it, First Peter commands it, and the qualifications for a church overseer include being hospitable, which means it is not a fringe activity but a mark of the faith itself. The word for seek in Romans 12 is a hunting word, pursue it, chase it down, which makes it active rather than a passive willingness to receive if someone happens to ask. The study clears away the idea that hospitality is a personality trait for outgoing people with big houses, because that idea has excused most of the church from a thing Scripture excuses no one from. What none of us is exempt from is the open door itself. The temperament and the house size are not the issue. The command is the same for the introvert in a small apartment as for anyone else, welcome the stranger.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is this not just religion recruiting through free meals?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study earns the right to answer it by refusing exactly that move. The hospitality it describes is explicitly a welcome extended to the one who cannot repay and without an agenda to fix or convert them first, the meal given freely, expecting nothing, precisely because a welcome that calculates a return is the thing Jesus attacked. If the open door is a recruitment tactic, it has already stopped being the thing Scripture means. What the study offers instead is a particular claim, that the deepest human need is to be welcomed rather than screened, seated rather than sorted, and that the writer himself was welcomed to a table while he was still an atheist, before he believed a word of it and with nothing asked in return. You do not have to share the faith to notice that a welcome given to people who can give nothing back is rarer and stranger than the reciprocal hospitality the world runs on, and to wonder what could possibly motivate it.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I am not naturally hospitable and my own door tends to stay shut?
faq.a: That is not a disqualification, it is your qualification, and it is the writer's too. The study was written to be led by ordinary people, not by gifted hosts, and every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer. The real qualification is not a naturally open home, which few people have, but a willingness to go first, to name your own fortress instinct and your own closed door and your own screening of strangers, and to keep the room safe for people who feel they are failing at this. If you present yourself as the hospitable expert, the room will admire you and change nothing, because admiration is the counterfeit of obedience and this is the easiest study in the world to enjoy and never obey. Your own struggle to open the door, honestly named, is the very thing that lets you stand inside the command alongside everyone else. Read the leader primer, name your own locked door, and go first.

timeline.event: Abraham runs from his tent in the heat of the day to welcome three strangers, mobilizing a feast for men he does not know, and entertains, unawares, the Lord himself with two angels, the founding story of biblical hospitality in Genesis 18.

The law given at Sinai binds Israel repeatedly to the sojourner, commanding that the stranger be treated as the native and loved as oneself, grounded in the memory that Israel too was once a stranger in Egypt, in Leviticus and Deuteronomy.

Isaiah names the fast God actually chooses, not private piety but an open house, sharing bread with the hungry and bringing the homeless poor inside, binding true worship to the welcome of the destitute.

Jesus keeps a table so scandalous that his reputation becomes a friend of tax collectors and sinners, eating with the unclean before they change, and teaches that welcoming the stranger is welcoming him, in the parables and the judgment of Matthew 25.

The early church, described in Acts, meets and eats in homes day by day, holding its goods loosely, and Paul lists hospitality among the marks of genuine Christian life, using a word that means to pursue the love of strangers.

Traveling teachers and persecuted believers depend entirely on the open homes of Christians, and the Didache and the letters of the New Testament treat hospitality as a basic obligation and a partnership in the truth itself.

Basil of Caesarea builds the Basileias, a complex for the poor, the sick, and the traveler on the edge of the city, institutionalizing Christian hospitality into organized care for the stranger and the destitute at a new scale.

The Rule of Benedict directs that every guest who arrives be received as Christ himself, embedding the welcome of the stranger into the daily life of the monastery and keeping a guest room and a washing of the guest's feet as sacred duty.

Monasteries, hospitals, and hostels across medieval Christendom carry the practice of welcoming the traveler and caring for the sick, the very word hospital and hostel and hospice descending from the Latin for the guest and the host.

Christine Pohl publishes Making Room: Recovering Hospitality as a Christian Tradition, recovering for a modern readership the long and demanding history of Christian welcome and naming what was lost when hospitality narrowed to private entertaining and impersonal service.

Henri Nouwen, in Reaching Out, reframes hospitality as the movement from hostility to welcome, the creation of a free and open space where the stranger can enter and become a friend without being forced to become like the host.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. Before we start, a word about what this study is and is not. It is not a discussion we can enjoy and then go home unchanged, and I am going to keep pulling us off the pleasant abstract idea of welcome and onto an actual stranger in an actual life, because that is the whole point. So expect to be asked, more than once, who the real lonely or foreign or overlooked person in your own life is. Second, this is not a study that shames anyone for a small home or a tired week. Hospitality is not entertaining, it never was, and a plain table in a plain room is exactly the thing Scripture means. And third, the writer stands inside all of this. He came to faith from atheism and was welcomed to a table before he believed a word of it, and he knows the reflex to keep the door shut because it is his own. We are not learning this from above it. We are learning it as people whose doors tend to stay closed. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what this session says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and onto the actual street each of us lives on, to a real person we could actually welcome or actually avoid, because none of this matters if the stranger stays an idea.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, and I am not going to tie it off with a neat plan, because the writer does not either, and hospitality is not a problem solved in an evening. Take the weight of this home rather than setting it down at the door. Try the practice this week, in your own home, with a real person, even awkwardly. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And come back ready to be honest, not finished. Remember, the test of this study is not whether we understood it but whether a door actually opened. Let me pray for us before we go, and I will see you next time.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the rule that admiration is not obedience, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, Philoxenia, Not the Dinner Party, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, Abraham, the Three Strangers, and Angels Unaware, with extended time on prudence and the closed door.
Week 4: Session 3, The Table Jesus Kept, part one, sitting with the scandal of who he ate with.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, the standards objection handled carefully and the practice of the uncomfortable guest list.
Week 6: Session 4, The Church as Household, on the home church and the privatized home.
Week 7: Session 5, The Cost of the Open Door, with the immigrant and the outsider named plainly and pastorally.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and the actual doors each member has opened or intends to, closing in the welcome of Christ.

bibliography.title: Making Room: Recovering Hospitality as a Christian Tradition
bibliography.author: Christine D. Pohl
bibliography.note: The scholarly and pastoral spine of the whole study, recovering the long history of Christian hospitality and naming what was lost when welcome narrowed to private entertaining and impersonal service. Anchors sessions 1, 4, and 5.

bibliography.title: Reaching Out: The Three Movements of the Spiritual Life
bibliography.author: Henri J. M. Nouwen
bibliography.note: The source of the reframing that hospitality is the movement from hostility to welcome, the creation of a free space where the stranger can enter and become a friend. Supports sessions 1 and 4. Leader to confirm specific phrasings before quoting.

bibliography.title: The Gospel Comes with a House Key: Practicing Radically Ordinary Hospitality in Our Post-Christian World
bibliography.author: Rosaria Butterfield
bibliography.note: A contemporary account of ordinary daily hospitality as the setting where the gospel becomes visible, useful for the household session and the cost of the open door. Supports sessions 4 and 5. A strong voice, leader to weigh against the study's frame.

bibliography.title: And You Welcomed Me: A Sourcebook on Hospitality in Early Christianity
bibliography.author: Amy G. Oden, editor
bibliography.note: A collection of early Christian texts on welcome, valuable background for the household session and the history of the practice. Supports session 4 and the timeline. Leader to draw on for primary sources rather than argument.

bibliography.title: The Meaning of Marriage
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Not on hospitality directly, but a model of the covenant-and-gospel frame this study applies, useful to leaders wanting the platform's method. Background only. Leader to confirm before attributing specific claims.

bibliography.title: Genesis
bibliography.author: the book of Genesis
bibliography.note: The primary text for session 2, where Abraham welcomes the three strangers at Mamre and Lot presses the angels to lodge with him against the inhospitality of Sodom. To be read and not only cited.

bibliography.title: The Gospel of Luke
bibliography.author: Luke the Evangelist
bibliography.note: The primary text for session 3, the Gospel that sets so much of Jesus's ministry at tables, from Levi's feast to Zacchaeus to the road to Emmaus. The heart of the study's account of the table Jesus kept, to be read straight through.

bibliography.title: Why Does He Do That? Inside the Minds of Angry and Controlling Men
bibliography.author: Lundy Bancroft
bibliography.note: Named so leaders handling the prudence and safety questions of session 2 can recognize genuine danger and distinguish it from ordinary discomfort. Background for wise, protective hospitality. Leader to pair with local resources.

furtherReading: Making Room, Christine Pohl, for anyone who wants the fuller history and theology of Christian hospitality behind sessions 1, 4, and 5.
Reaching Out, Henri Nouwen, for those who want to sit longer with hospitality as the inner movement from hostility to welcome, leader to confirm specific phrasings.
The Gospel Comes with a House Key, Rosaria Butterfield, for readers who want a contemporary, practical picture of ordinary daily hospitality, read alongside the study's covenant frame.
Genesis 18 and 19, read together, for the founding story of welcome and its violent refusal, the material behind session 2.
The Gospel of Luke, read with attention to every meal, for those willing to see how thoroughly Jesus set the kingdom at a table, the material behind session 3.

glossary.definition: The Greek word the New Testament uses for hospitality, built from phileo, to love, and xenos, the stranger. Love of the stranger, not love of the guest list you already have, and the specific virtue Romans, Hebrews, and First Peter command of the whole church.

The Greek word for stranger, foreigner, or guest, the one who is not yet a friend and cannot repay you. The object of the love in philoxenia, and the person Scripture keeps naming as the one welcome is actually for.

The modern substitute for hospitality, a performance staged in a presentable home for guests who can return the favor, running quietly on reciprocity. A real good in the feast of friends, but not the command, and not to be confused with the welcome of the stranger.

The ger, the resident foreigner or immigrant, named more than thirty times in the law as an object of God's particular care. Israel is commanded to love the sojourner because Israel was itself a sojourner in Egypt, the memory grounding the command.

The phrase from Hebrews 13, drawn from Abraham at Mamre, naming not a promise that every stranger is secretly wonderful but the truth that we cannot see in advance what a welcome will become, which removes our excuse for turning the ordinary stranger away.

The quiet economy Jesus attacked, the invitation extended expecting to be repaid, the welcome given as an investment. The instinct that closes the circle of the table, and the thing grace breaks by welcoming the one who cannot pay anything back.

The scholarly term for Jesus's practice of eating across every social boundary his culture policed, sharing tables with tax collectors and sinners and the unclean. A lived parable that the God he proclaimed does not sort his guests the way society sorts its tables.

Paul's phrase for the church, and for its first three hundred years a literal household, meeting and eating and welcoming the stranger in homes rather than buildings. A household with the accent on the second word, where the open door was the shape of the thing.

The modern privatized home understood as a defended retreat, a place to shut the world out, which the early church would not recognize. Not a lifestyle preference only but a spiritual condition, the closed door the study keeps pressing against.

The false measure that turns hospitality into an impressive home and a flawless meal, and so stops more welcome than selfishness does, because those who cannot host beautifully decide not to host at all. The good made the enemy of the commanded.

Christine Pohl's image and Nouwen's, the self-emptying that clears a free space for the stranger to enter, which the introvert and the poor can do as well as anyone, because it is not about impressive hosting but about an inner poverty that has room for another.

The truth the study refuses to sentimentalize, that every real welcome costs the host something, time, comfort, safety, the tidy life, and that a welcome costing nothing was never the thing Scripture meant, because the welcome we received was paid for at infinite cost.

The wise limit that protects a genuinely generous life, and also the most fluent modern excuse, the language of self-care laid over a door that was already shut. The study asks the reader to tell the real limit from the wall that only calls itself one.
